name: pixelbolt-pixel-art
description: Make, fix and export pixel art sprites, tiles, effects and short animations from JSON recipes
readme: # Pixelbolt [](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/gallery/) **[The gallery](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/gallery/): 66 pixel art effects, sprites and scenes from Pixelbolt 0.11.0, all playing, each one click from its recipe in the playground.** Give Claude Code the pixel art skill in one line (Node.js 20 or newer): ```sh npx -y pixelbolt@latest skill install ``` For Codex, Cursor and the other agents the open [skills CLI](https://skills.sh) supports: `npx skills add skulitom/Pixelbolt`. It copies the skill file alone, which then runs Pixelbolt through npx. The CLI reports installs to the skills.sh leaderboard unless `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` is set. The skills CLI needs Node.js 22.20 or newer. **Pixel art and sprite animation that your AI agent can make, check and fix.** Pixelbolt turns an editable JSON recipe into sprites, tiles, icons, effects and short animations, and exports them as PNG sprite sheets, texture atlases, animated PNGs, GIFs and frames for a video editor. Agents drive it through a local MCP server or the command line; you can open, play and edit the same recipe in a local browser studio. [Try it in your browser](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/playground/): render, export and share recipes with nothing installed. [Pixel art explosion generator](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/playground/explosion-generator/): pick one of three explosions, tweak its recipe, and download a PNG sprite sheet, a GIF, or a sheet with an atlas JSON. [Poke the pixels](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/playground/fluids/): blow on a live pixel-art campfire, pour honey and slime, then save a GIF or share a link that replays exactly what you did. [Effect guides](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/guides/): fire, explosions, smoke and steam, water, slime and honey, and magic, each with recipes that open in the playground. Using Unreal Engine? [Import the sheets into Paper2D, with flipbooks](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/guides/unreal-paper2d-sprite-sheets/) (tested in 5.8.4). Need ground tiles? [Free autotile tile sets for Godot 4 and Tiled](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/guides/tileset-generator-godot-tiled/), drawn from a terrain description (tested in Godot 4.7.2 and Tiled 1.12.2). Just want files? [Six free pixel art waterfall sprite sheets](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/guides/pixel-art-waterfall-animation/): one simulated waterfall in stone, lava, slime and moonlit, with Godot 4 files. [Neon Voyage](https://skulitom.github.io/NeonRocketGame/): a free browser game made with Pixelbolt. Every sprite, effect and letter is a [recipe](https://github.com/skulitom/NeonRocketGame/tree/main/art), and the rocket's exhaust is a live fluid simulation that bends as you steer. **Who it's for:** game developers, game-jam teams and web or video makers who want an agent such as Claude, Codex or Cursor to draw and revise their pixel art, and people building agents that need exact, repeatable images. - **Use it when** you want small 2D game assets that stay editable as text: the agent reads every pixel back, fixes one pixel or one frame without redrawing the rest, and the same recipe renders the same image every time. - **Don't use it for** painted or photographic images, large animations (an animation frame is at most 1024 pixels a side and 262,144 pixels, such as 320 × 180, 640 × 360 or 512 × 512, and a project at most 256 frames and 4,194,304 pixels in all, so 72 frames of 320 × 180; a single still, such as a 1920 × 1080 backdrop or mural, may be up to 4096 pixels a side within that total), generating art with an image model, or editing GIFs and Aseprite files (it imports PNG only, at up to 8 bits per channel). - **Compared with** aseprite-mcp, pixel-mcp, pixscii, pixelart-mcp, pixelforge-mcp and SpriteCook, with Pixelbolt's measured runs, the others read from their code and docs, and when to choose each one instead: [Pixel art and sprite tools for AI agents: 7 MCP servers compared](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/compare/pixel-art-mcp-servers-for-ai-agents/) (checked 17 October 2026; refreshed 11 November with 0.15.0 measured). For fire, smoke, explosion, water and spell effects, with Pixel FX Designer, SpriteMancer, Fluid FX, Pixel Composer, PHOSPHOR, BlastFX, Pixel VFX Forge, Codixel and pixelfx: [Pixel FX Designer alternatives: 10 tools compared](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/compare/pixel-fx-designer-alternatives/) (checked 19 October 2026; Codixel added and Pixelbolt re-measured on 0.17.0 on 15 November; pixelfx added and run on 17 November). Measured with and without Pixelbolt on Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5, in a benchmark we planned in advance: [Does a pixel-art MCP server help Claude?](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/compare/claude-pixel-art-with-and-without-pixelbolt/) (run 23 October to 3 November 2026; on 0.11.0, 32 of 36 runs passed every check with Pixelbolt and 31 without, blind pairs 18 to 13 with one by default, p = 0.47, at 1.47 times the cost, short of our rule for saying it helps; animations and effects, which 0.11.0 was built for, 9 of 15 pairs, p = 0.61, and a same-day repeat would have failed that bar). For ring-escape, bouncing-ball and territory battle Shorts, with BallTok, Satisfying Labs, BounceMatch, ReelBall, BallSimulator, BallEngine, Korpi, WaveSpeed's free maker and physim: [Ring escape and territory battle Shorts with a free, open-source simulator](https://skulitom.github.io/Pixelbolt/compare/ring-escape-and-territory-battle-shorts/) (checked 9 November 2026; two clips with their recipes and one command each). **Try it.** You need Node.js 20 or newer; there is nothing else to install, no API key and no network service: ```sh git clone https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt.git cd Pixelbolt node bin/pixelbolt.js preview --open ``` No Node.js? [Download Pixelbolt Studio](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/releases/latest): a portable build for Windows, macOS and Linux that brings its own Node.js runtime. Unpack it and start the studio; nothing is installed ([portable builds](#pixelbolt-studio-portable-builds)). **Give it to your agent.** For Claude Code, one line installs the pixel art skill, with nothing to clone and no MCP server (Pixelbolt 0.9.2 or later): ```sh npx -y pixelbolt@latest skill install ``` It writes `~/.claude/skills/pixelbolt-pixel-art/` (`--project` writes the current folder's `.claude/skills/` instead, `--dir` any skills folder), runs every command it names through `npx -y pixelbolt@`, and never replaces a copy you have changed unless you add `--force`. For Pixelbolt's MCP tools too, install the [Claude Code plugin](#connect-an-agent-through-mcp) instead: it brings the server and the same skill together. In Claude Desktop, download [`pixelbolt.mcpb`](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/releases/latest/download/pixelbolt.mcpb) from the latest release and open it (or install it from file under Settings → Extensions), choose a workspace folder for recipes and artwork, then ask the agent to call `pixel_help`. For Codex, Cursor and other MCP clients, see [Connect an agent through MCP](#connect-an-agent-through-mcp). Pixelbolt is in the official MCP Registry as `io.github.skulitom/pixelbolt`. Pixelbolt was called PixelForge until 0.8.0. The `pixelforge` command still works as an alias, and recipe files keep their `pixelforge-*` format tags, so existing files and agent setups keep working. [Gallery](#gallery) · [Fluid effects](#fluid-effects) · [Quick start](#start) · [Agent setup](#for-agents) · [MCP server](#connect-an-agent-through-mcp) · [Portable builds](#pixelbolt-studio-portable-builds) · [Recipe reference](docs/agent-guide.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Sibling tools](#sibling-tools) ## How it works Write a JSON recipe with palettes, text grids, reusable symbols and drawing operations. Get transparent PNGs, sprite sheets, animated PNGs, GIFs for sharing, numbered frames for video editors, and the metadata and player needed to use them. Inspect and edit the recipe in a local browser studio. Zero runtime dependencies. No build step, API key, image model, network service or native graphics library. Requires **Node.js 20 or newer**. Works from a checkout on Windows, macOS and Linux. ## Figures in motion Author limbs as bones, bodies as masses, and faces or props as grids. Relative joints and two-bone reach keep attachments together; idle, walk, run, jump, attack and hurt templates expand into editable poses. Review planted feet, ground contact and loop joins in the CLI, MCP or studio. Small grid parts (boots, hands, blades) turn best as hand-drawn `views`; `--draft-views` drafts them by pixel-art rules for you to correct and paste. The output uses the existing sprite player. ```sh node bin/pixelbolt.js preview character.poses.json node bin/pixelbolt.js compile character.poses.json --expand --out character-edit.poses.json node bin/pixelbolt.js compile character.poses.json --draft-views boot:15,345,hand:45 --preview drafts.png node bin/pixelbolt.js inspect character.poses.json --motion run --speed 48 ``` [Pose and motion reference](docs/art-workflow.md#structural-limbs-and-bodies) ## Baked wave effects Looping interference and portal interiors combine waves before colouring them, leaving cancellation gaps between bright bands. Two editable presets bake to ordinary sprite frames and appear in the studio's sample list. The game only plays the exported animation. ![Paired cyan waves and a violet portal in a Tidewatch game scene](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/waves/scene.gif) ```sh node bin/pixelbolt.js preview examples/portal.wave.json --open node bin/pixelbolt.js compile examples/portal.wave.json --out output/portal.json node bin/pixelbolt.js render output/portal.json --out output/portal-assets ``` [Wave controls and limits](docs/wave-effects.md) · [Scene comparison and review](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/blob/main/showcase/waves/README.md). Loops only; masks shape the artwork without simulating reflection or collision. ## Made with Pixelbolt: Tetherbore [](https://skulitom.github.io/Tetherbore/) **[Play Tetherbore](https://skulitom.github.io/Tetherbore/)**, a free one-thumb mining game for the phone browser. Every sprite, tile set and effect in it, across all of its grounds, creatures and bosses, is made with Pixelbolt from [recipes in its repository](https://github.com/skulitom/Tetherbore/tree/master/art). ## Gallery An AI agent drew these with Pixelbolt. Its scripts write the recipes, particle sources and scenes; Pixelbolt renders every sprite to a transparent sheet with an atlas, plays each 240×135 room as a scene and writes the GIFs. They are shown at 3×. ![An observatory: a porthole onto a ringed planet, a telescope, an armillary with a blooming crystal and a cat asleep on the window seat](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/gallery/observatory.gif) ![A workshop: a half-built brass automaton, a gear clock, glass coils that arc and a clockwork mouse](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/gallery/workshop.gif) ![Eight potions, each popping its cork: green, red, blue, purple, orange, frost, shadow and rainbow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/gallery/potions.gif) ![Four bell jars: a sprouting bloom, glowcap mushrooms, a snapping flytrap and a succulent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/gallery/bell-jars.gif) ![Three clockwork familiars: a brass owl, a koi in its bowl and a crystal moth over a lantern](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/main/showcase/gallery/familiars.gif) [Two more rooms and how these were made](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/blob/main/showcase/gallery/README.md) ## Fluid effects A `pixelforge-fluid` source runs a small, deterministic fluid simulation and compiles it into an ordinary recipe of palette grids: gases with buoyancy, swirling vorticity, cooling and dissipation, and liquids as FLIP particles on the same grid, thin as water, thick as honey (a stream that never breaks, a mound that slowly sinks) or firm as slime (a blob that squashes, springs back and holds its shape). Look layers map density, temperature, speed and depth onto your palette ramps through ordered dither, so no colour outside the palette can appear, and looping effects close their seam. Each preset below compiles in well under a second on a laptop CPU, with no GPU and no model calls. In the studio, **Fluid lab** (`/fluid.html`) runs the same compiler in your browser: pick a preset, move a few sliders and download the GIF, sprite sheet, recipe or edited source. **Effects lab** (`/effects.html`) does the same for the `pixelforge-fx` spell and particle presets: pick one of a source's effects (turned copies included), change its strength, speed and seed, and download. The [fluid effects guide](docs/art-workflow.md#fluid-effects) covers emitters, sparks, obstacles, looks, loops, thick fluids (viscosity, yield stress, adhesion), sticky liquids that move with an obstacle and stretch into strings, and electricity. In a web page, `createLiveFluid` runs the same simulation live, a frame at a time, and takes pushes, puffs and emitter boosts from the pointer ([live fluids](docs/art-workflow.md#live-fluids)). ## Rigid bodies A `pixelforge-bodies` source drops balls, boxes, polygons and spinning hoops into a canvas with gravity, walls and drawn pixel obstacles: they bounce, slide, roll, stack, knock each other about and come to rest, baked into palette grids like every other compiler. A body can start asleep until it is hit, change colour at each hit, trail behind it or be drawn as a sprite. Joints connect bodies into ragdolls, ropes sag and break, and cloth pins to bodies, ripples in the wind, drapes and tears. On a territory of team-owned cells, each team's balls claim the other side's cells they hit, with pickups that split, grow, speed up, warp or pull, a live score drawn over the board, and long matches written straight to video frames. A strike gives a power to whatever a named body touches, so a sword turning about its hilt can split every ball it hits until the crowd fills its ring. Sources stay editable JSON. ### GIF for sharing APNG keeps full alpha and exact timing, but many chat, forum and store pages only animate GIFs and cannot scale pixels crisply. `pixelbolt gif` writes one animation as a GIF at the frames' own size; `--scale` (1-16) enlarges it by a whole number for pages that would show a small sprite tiny: ```sh node bin/pixelbolt.js gif hero.pixel.json --out hero.gif node bin/pixelbolt.js gif --preset campfire --size 32x32 --scale 8 --out campfire.gif --sheet campfire-frames.png node bin/pixelbolt.js gif hero.pixel.json --animation blink --scale 8 --background "#17191d" --out hero-blink.gif ``` Colours are exact: nothing is quantized or dithered, and a frame that needs more than 256 colours is refused with an error instead of being approximated. GIF has no partial transparency, so pixels below 50% alpha become transparent and the rest opaque; `--background` (a palette name or opaque hex colour) blends every pixel onto one colour instead, which keeps soft shadows. Frame times are rounded to GIF's 10 ms steps with the remainder carried to the next frame, and raised to 20 ms where shorter. Transparent pixels stay clear in every viewer, including ffmpeg and Pillow, which fill a cleared frame with the background colour unless it names a transparent index (the notes report the rare frame with 256 colours of its own that has none to name). The JSON result's `notes` say which of these happened. The studio's **GIF** button downloads the current animation at the current zoom, and MCP `pixel_render` takes `"gif": {}` (the frames' own size) or `"gif": { "scale": 8 }`. Every render also reports a `check` of what it wrote; give `pixel_render` an `expect` (or `render` an `--expect`) with the size, frames, colours, background or loop the user asked for, and the check names each file that misses it and how to fix it. The export bundle itself is unchanged. `pixelbolt gif-frames` makes a GIF from a folder of numbered PNG frames, such as a `sequence` folder or frames a video or effects tool wrote, by the same rules: ```sh node bin/pixelbolt.js gif-frames shots/prism --fps 25 --out prism.gif node bin/pixelbolt.js gif-frames shots/prism --fps 30 --loops 3 --background "#101828" --prefix prism_ --out prism-3x.gif ``` Files are read in number order (`prism_0001.png`, `prism_0002.png` …); gaps in the numbering, other PNGs in the folder and a folder holding two sequences (choose one with `--prefix`) are reported, never guessed around. Each frame keeps its exact colours: one with more than 256 is refused by name, and when the frames use different colours, each frame carries a colour table of its own, so a loop of 48 frames at 1080 × 1080 with about 120 colours per frame and 4,345 in all decodes back pixel for pixel, where a palette generator would shift some colours. Frame k starts at k × 1000 / fps ms rounded to GIF's centiseconds: 25 fps is 40 ms per frame, 30 fps alternates 30 and 40 ms and keeps the loop's length, and above 50 fps delays are raised to 20 ms, which the notes report with the new length. `--loops` is the number of plays, 0 (the default) for ever. Without transparency, each frame after the first stores only the rectangle that changed. The PNGs may be RGB, RGBA, greyscale or indexed with up to 8 bits per channel, all the same size; the loop may hold 134,217,728 pixels (115 frames at 1080 × 1080). ### Pixel text The `text` operation draws titles, captions, labels and counters in a built-in pixel font: printable ASCII, the accented letters of western European languages (À–ÿ, Œ œ Š š Ž ž Ÿ), Cyrillic, Japanese kana, every Korean Hangul syllable, 165 ideographs of game menus (開始, 設定, 魔法 …) and common symbols such as € £ © — … “ ” „ « », with capitals 7 pixels tall, proportional letters and tabular digits. Hangul and ideographs are drawn in a 9×9 cell. The accent of a capital sits in the two rows above `y`. ```json { "op": "text", "x": 120, "y": 8, "text": "GAME OVER\nscore 12480", "color": "ink", "align": "center" } ``` `align` says whether `x` is the left edge, the centre or the right edge; `spacing`, `lineHeight`, `scale` and rotation adjust it, and `outline` after it gives a readable edge. Text that runs off the canvas is reported like any other clipped drawing, and a character the font lacks is an error that names it. [examples/caption.json](examples/caption.json) is a lower third that opens and types its title; `node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence examples/caption.json --fps 30 --size 1080p --align bottom --offset 0,-64 --out shots/caption` turns it into 81 frames that sit across the bottom of a 1080p picture. ### Frames for a video editor Video editors do not animate APNG, and GIF loses alpha and exact timing. `pixelbolt sequence` writes what editors do read: one numbered PNG per video frame, at a constant frame rate, on a canvas of the video's size, with the alpha kept. ```sh node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence hero.pixel.json --fps 30 --size 1080p --out shots/hero node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence examples/effects.fx.json --animation sparks --fps 29.97 --size 4k --scale 16 --align bottom --offset 0,-200 --out shots/sparks node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence room.scene.json --fps 24 --size 1080p --fit cover --out shots/room ``` - **Timing.** Each video frame shows the pose that is active when the frame starts. `--fps` takes 24, 25, 30, 50, 60, the NTSC rates 23.976, 29.97 and 59.94 (kept exact as 24000/1001, 30000/1001 and 60000/1001, so long clips do not drift), or a fraction. `--loops n` or `--seconds s` sets the length; `--step 2` animates on twos. A looping animation keeps cycling; one that plays once holds its last pose. - **Size.** `--size` is `720p`, `1080p`, `1440p`, `4k`, `vertical` (1080×1920), `square` or `WIDTHxHEIGHT`. The sprite is enlarged by a whole number, never resampled: the largest that fits, or `--scale` up to 256. `--align` (`top-left` … `center` … `bottom-right`) and `--offset x,y` place it. `--fit cover` takes the smallest whole number that covers the canvas instead and crops what hangs over; `--align` then chooses the part that stays, and the result's `placement.visible` says which columns and rows of the source that is. Without `--size` the canvas is the sprite at `--scale`. `--background` blends onto an opaque colour instead of keeping alpha. - **Sources.** A recipe (`--animation` picks one), a pose, autotile or effects source, which is compiled on the way in, or a scene, which is rendered moment by moment as a shot; moments that look the same share one PNG. A scene of 192×108 or 240×135 pixels fills 1080p exactly at scale 10 or 8. Any other scene is centred with margins in its own background colour, so the shot is still opaque from edge to edge, or fills the canvas with `--fit cover`. - **What you get.** A new folder with `name_0001.png` onwards, `sequence.json` (frame rate as a fraction, frame count, size, placement, loop facts and the timing of every pose) and a `README.txt` that says how to import them. The result's `notes` say what the frame grid did: which poses changed length, which are shorter than a video frame and never shown, and whether the clip ends exactly where the loop does, with the number of loops that would. - **One video file.** Pixelbolt does not encode video. The folder's README and the JSON result give the exact `ffmpeg` command for a ProRes 4444 `.mov` with alpha, and, when there is a background, for an H.264 `.mp4` in lossless 4:4:4. H.264 usually stores colour once for each 2 × 2 pixels (4:2:0), which smears every pixel edge whatever the scale once a player interpolates it; 4:4:4 keeps every colour, in a file no larger for pixel art, but QuickTime, Safari and Windows' own players may not play it, so on an even canvas `h264Compatible` gives a 4:2:0 file as well. With ffmpeg 7 the ProRes command keeps the alpha exactly and the colours within 2 of 255, and the H.264 command the colours within 1; `scripts/verify-exports.py` repeats those checks when ffmpeg is installed. In the editor, import the files as an image sequence and set the clip's frame rate (the files carry none), then leave the clip at 100% scale: scaling there would blur the pixels. A sequence holds at most 18,000 frames and a canvas at most 4096 pixels on a side. MCP `pixel_render` and `pixel_scene` take `"sequence": { "fps": 30, "size": "1080p" }` with the same options. The studio's **Frames** button downloads the same files for the animation on screen as one ZIP. Its dialog also shows the `pixelbolt sequence` command and the MCP `sequence` argument for the chosen frame rate and size, so an agent can repeat the export without the browser. ### Large frames and stills An animation frame may be up to 1024 pixels a side and 262,144 pixels: a full-screen 320 × 180, 480 × 270 or 640 × 360 overlay (rain, snow, fog) is one recipe, as is a 512 × 512 or 1024 × 256 frame. All of a recipe's frames hold at most 4,194,304 pixels, so 72 frames of 320 × 180, 18 of 640 × 360 or 16 of 512 × 512. A recipe with a single frame may be larger still: up to 4096 pixels a side and 4,194,304 pixels in all. A 1920 × 1080 or 2560 × 1440 backdrop, wallpaper or mural is then one canvas, drawn at one screen pixel per art pixel, and every drawing operation sees all of it. On a canvas wider or taller than 256, rectangles, ellipses and dither or shade regions may be up to twice its side instead of 512. A scene's view and each of its assets, an effect source and an imported frame have the animation frame's limit, so a tiled level is one picture. Everything else keeps its limits: pose, bodies, crystal, normals and compiled powder sources stay at 256 pixels a side, fluid and wave sources at 128, and the 67-million-pixel drawing budget is unchanged: `fill`, `replace` and `outline` each pass over the whole canvas, about 2 million of that budget at 1920 × 1080. To show bigger pixels instead, enlarge a small canvas with `sheet.scale` or `sequence --size`, as before. Add it to your agent's MCP configuration and replace `/absolute/path/to/pixelbolt-output` with the folder where exports should go. Use an absolute path, because clients start servers in different folders; on Windows use forward slashes, for example `C:/Art/pixelbolt-output`: ```json { "mcpServers": { "pixelbolt": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "pixelbolt@latest", "mcp", "--out", "/absolute/path/to/pixelbolt-output"] } } } ``` For clients that use TOML: ```toml [mcp_servers.pixelbolt] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "pixelbolt@latest", "mcp", "--out", "/absolute/path/to/pixelbolt-output"] ``` On Windows, a client that starts the server without a shell can't run `npx` (Kimi Code reports `spawn npx ENOENT`). Use `"command": "cmd"` with `"args": ["/c", "npx", "-y", "pixelbolt@latest", "mcp", "--out", "C:/Art/pixelbolt-output"]` there instead. To run a checkout instead (for example `main`, which can be ahead of npm), clone the repository and use `"command": "node"` with `"args": ["/absolute/path/to/Pixelbolt/bin/pixelbolt.js", "mcp", "--out", "/absolute/path/to/Pixelbolt/output"]`. **Kimi Code, DeepSeek Harness and OpenCode.** Each takes the same `npx` server in its own format: - **Kimi Code CLI:** put the `mcpServers` block above in `~/.kimi-code/mcp.json` (or `.kimi-code/mcp.json` in a trusted project), in the `cmd /c` form on Windows; `/mcp` shows it. - **OpenCode:** add it under `mcp` in `opencode.json` (the project's, or `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`), with the whole command as one array; `opencode mcp list` shows it connected: ```json { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "mcp": { "pixelbolt": { "type": "local", "command": ["npx", "-y", "pixelbolt@latest", "mcp", "--out", "/absolute/path/to/pixelbolt-output"] } } } ``` - **DeepSeek Harness:** add this to `~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml`; the tools appear as `mcp__pixelbolt__pixel_render` and so on: ```yaml - insert: - id: mcp-pixelbolt name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client' config: serverName: pixelbolt transport: stdio command: npx args: ['-y', 'pixelbolt@latest', 'mcp', '--out', '/absolute/path/to/pixelbolt-output'] env: {} ``` All three also read skills from `~/.agents/skills/`, so `npx -y pixelbolt@latest skill install --dir "$HOME/.agents/skills"` gives them the pixel art skill as well (in cmd.exe, `--dir "%USERPROFILE%\.agents\skills"`). Checked on 3 November 2026 with Pixelbolt 0.11.0 on Windows: OpenCode 1.19.5 lists the server as connected; Kimi Code 2.4.1 finds all eight tools through `cmd /c` (a bare `npx` fails there); DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1-rc.5 accepts the patch, though the server wasn't started from it, because it needs a DeepSeek key to start. The eight tools are: - **`pixel_help`**: a short quick start (the recipe format, operations, tools and workflow, about 2,000 tokens); `topic` returns the full authoring guide (`guide`), the art workflow (`workflow`), the recipe schema (`schema`), a complete sample (`example`), or the stack, poses, scenes, autotile, fx, fluid, wave, crystal, powder, bodies or normals schemas (the guide and workflow list their sections, and `name` returns one, a part of a long one, or the paragraphs that mention a word); topic `presets` lists the shipped presets (fire, smoke, explosions, spells, liquids, plasma, rigid bodies, crystals, falling sand, characters) to compile instead of drawing, and `preset` with `name` returns one's source. - **`pixel_validate`**: validate `{ "project": ... }` and save its recipe revision without exporting assets. Reports every clipped location; `"fps": 30` adds `frameGrid`, the durations off that video frame grid and what a sequence would do to each animation. - **`pixel_inspect`**: contact sheets, exact regional grids, silhouette/grayscale/onion views, a parts view naming the layer or pose part behind each pixel, 3×3 tile repeats with seam evidence, native size, named layer isolation, saved-reference comparisons, advisory diagnostics, motion review with contacts, limb arcs and explicit pose metadata, and perspective `guides` (a horizon, vanishing points, an isometric grid). `frames` takes `*`/`?` patterns, `step`/`offset` keep every nth cell, and optional bounded samples expose omissions. Saves its recipe revision. - **`pixel_patch`**: apply targeted `set`, `insert`, `remove` and `paint` edits. For example, `{ "paint": "frames[blink]", "value": [{ "x": 9, "y": 7, "color": "k" }] }` corrects a pixel in final canvas coordinates after all layers; `transparent` erases it. Returns every frame whose pixels changed (exact pixels for small edits) and a before/after PNG. The source stays unchanged and successful edits get a new revision. - **`pixel_render`**: render `{ "project": ... }`, return a PNG contact sheet of every frame with cell names/timing plus the output folder, its key files and frame/animation counts (`listFiles: true` lists everything). Add `"animation": "idle"` to preview a sequence in playback order. The exported APNGs and HTML preview play the animation. Add `"gif": {}` (or `{ "scale": 8, "background": "#17191d" }`) to also write every animation as a GIF in `gifs/`, with notes on any alpha or timing change, and `"sequence": { "fps": 30, "size": "1080p" }` to write one animation as numbered PNG frames for a video editor in `sequence/`. Every call writes a fresh folder inside the configured output directory. - **`pixel_compile`**: compile a `pixelforge-poses` source (including bones, masses, relative joints, reach targets and editable motion templates), a `pixelforge-autotile` template or terrain (returned with a second image of every tile over a test map), a `pixelforge-fx` source (particles and spell shapes), a `pixelforge-fluid` source (simulated smoke, fire, explosions, magic, water, thick and sticky liquids, sand, air pockets and bubbles, ice and steam, electric arcs, and bodies that float, sink and stir), a `pixelforge-wave` source (looping interference and portals), a `pixelforge-crystal` source (crystals, clusters, geodes and snowflakes that grow and rest), a `pixelforge-powder` source (a falling-sand sandbox of sand, water, fire, smoke, lava and more, sampled into one-shot clips), a `pixelforge-bodies` source (balls, boxes and hoops that bounce, stack and rest, and territory matches; `sequence` writes a match of any length as numbered video frames) or a `pixelforge-normals` source (a normal pass derived from a recipe or revision, with flat `faces` by colour for boxes and walls) into a recipe revision, with a contact sheet and optional metadata; `preset` compiles a shipped preset by name instead of a `source`. - **`pixel_scene`**: render a `pixelforge-scene` manifest (tilemaps with autotile legends and neighbour rules, named cues, sequences, trajectories, attachments, ground sorting, shade placements, ramp or multiplied lighting from point lights and a sun, with cast shadows, palette themes, haze for far planes, a panning camera with parallax planes) at any time, with a `depth` view of what is drawn in front of what, export it (with a Tiled map of it whose layers carry each plane's parallax, `scene.tmx`, hazed copies of far assets, and each plane as an image that a Godot `scene.tscn` scrolls with `Parallax2D`), or write it as a shot of numbered PNG frames with `sequence`; assets may be revisions. - **`pixel_import`**: import a native-resolution PNG, given as base64 or a file inside the server root, as a lossless recipe revision. `pixel_render` optionally accepts `"share": true` for a playground link (or a link-limit error without failing the render) and `"embedRecipe": true` for recipes inside exported PNGs. `pixel_render` also writes files at the names the user asked for: `"saveAs": { "sheet": "assets/hero.png", "gif": "assets/hero.gif" }` (keys `sheet`, `atlas`, `godot` for the Godot `.tres`, `tileset` for an autotile set's Godot TileSet, `tiled` for its Tiled tileset, `recipe`, `gif`, `apng` or any exported PNG, GIF or JSON file; paths inside the server root, keeping the file type, never under a hidden name or in the home folder's `AppData` or `Library`). A saved atlas, `.tres` or `.tsx` names the saved sheet (or the export folder's), and a `.tres` inside a Godot project needs its sheet inside it too. It never replaces an existing file unless `"overwrite": true`, and then a JSON file only if it is a recipe, atlas or sequence, a `.tres` only if it is the same kind of Godot resource (SpriteFrames, TileSet or CanvasTexture), and a `.tsx` only if it is a Tiled tileset; it never writes over the palette and asset files the recipe references, and checks every path before writing anything. `pixel_patch` also supports compact `grid`, masked `move`, regional `recolor` and proposed `cleanup` of doubled corners and stray pixels, with explicit `frame` or `inherited` scope, and applies saved correction overlays (`overlay`). Large `pixel_render` previews are sampled with total/shown/omitted metadata instead of blocking a valid export; exported animations remain complete. Palette and scene file references resolve inside the server's `--root` (default: its working directory); requests may be up to 16 MiB, and an oversized request is answered with an error without stopping the server. Each tool call runs in a worker thread and is stopped if it takes longer than 50 seconds (`--time-limit ` changes this) or runs out of memory; the call is answered with an error that says so, and the server keeps serving. A `sequence` from one call may come to at most 512 MB; `pixelbolt sequence` writes longer shots. Send a recipe once. Each successful recipe-tool response includes a `revision` id that the other tools accept in place of `project`, so later calls, including patches, need not resend the recipe. Validate, inspect, patch and render save immutable snapshots in `/.revisions/`; they survive restarts when you use the same directory, even before an asset export. Once that directory exists, the presets listing keeps what it measured in `.presets/` beside them, so later listings are quick. Prefer an absolute `--out` path. Earlier revisions remain undo points. Older rendered revisions can be recovered from saved bundle recipes. Render also saves the recipe beside the assets. The server implements newline-delimited stdio MCP with initialization, version negotiation, ping and tool discovery/calls. It supports protocol versions 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25 through initialization, plus 2026-07-28 through `server/discover` and stateless requests carrying protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`. It uses no HTTP transport or external services. See the [MCP stdio specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports). An agent can also use the CLI directly. The reusable [agent skill](skills/pixelbolt-pixel-art/SKILL.md) and [authoring reference](docs/agent-guide.md) explain the complete format; `npx -y pixelbolt@latest skill install` gives Claude Code the skill with its guides, schemas and examples and no server. [schema.json](schema.json) supports editor completion and structural validation; the rasterizer additionally validates references, matching row widths and resource limits. ## Inline previews (MCP Apps) Hosts that support MCP Apps (the `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` extension) show an inline pixel art player for inspect, patch, compile, render, scene and import results. It has crisp integer zoom, playback, frame stepping, speed, animation and background controls; render results also show written paths, the delivery check and an optional playground button. The viewer needs no network. Clients without MCP Apps receive exactly the same tool listings and results as before. ## Use in a web app Serve the exported folder with your application: ```html ``` Or use CSS alone: ```html ``` CSS honors reduced-motion preferences. The Canvas API leaves autoplay decisions to the application. Atlas paths in `SpritePlayer.load` resolve relative to the atlas URL. A game drawing many sprites into one canvas can use the same module's helpers. `drawFrame` places a frame by its anchor (when the recipe declares one), restores trimmed frames to their original offset and snaps fractional positions to whole pixels, so a sprite moving at sub-pixel speeds keeps hard edges. `rotate` (radians, about the anchor) turns it. A turned sprite keeps clean square pixels only where each of its pixels covers several of the canvas's, so draw what turns, and what should glide from place to place and not step, on a second canvas at the screen's own resolution with `scale` 3 or more, laid over the canvas the grid-aligned world is drawn on: ```html ``` For Godot 4, put `name.png` and `name.tres` in one folder of the project and use the `.tres` as an `AnimatedSprite2D`'s Sprite Frames, or install the [Godot addon](docs/game-integration.md#the-editor-addon-recipes-as-spriteframes), which imports `*.pixel.json` recipes as SpriteFrames and renders them again when they change. For another engine, use the atlas rectangles or individual PNGs. For regular-grid importers, set `sheet.padding` to `0` and use the exported frame dimensions. Phaser accepts the JSON-hash frame layout via `load.atlas`; named animation sequences are in the extra `animations` field. See [game integration notes](docs/game-integration.md). ## JavaScript API ```js import { renderProject, inspectProject, patchRecipe, compareProjects, createBundle, writeBundle, readExpect, checkDelivery, compileEffects, compileFluid, createLiveFluid, animationGIF, folderGIF, frameGrid } from './src/index.js'; const project = renderProject(recipe); // RGBA buffers, durations, warnings const view = inspectProject(project, { grid: true }); // contact sheet RGBA, palette-key grids const { recipe: next, edits } = patchRecipe(recipe, [{ set: 'frames[idle].duration', value: 120 }]); const report = compareProjects(project, renderProject(next)); // changed pixels, timing, before/after RGBA const bundle = await createBundle(recipe); await writeBundle(bundle, './output/my-sprite'); const check = checkDelivery(bundle.project, { recipe, expect: readExpect({ width: 32, height: 32, frames: 8 }) }); // the CLI's and MCP's check: { ok, delivered, problems }, each problem with its fix const { recipe: effects } = compileEffects(fxSource); // seeded particles and spell shapes baked into an ordinary recipe const { recipe: fire, metadata } = compileFluid(fluidSource); // a fluid simulation baked into palette grids const { rgba, keys } = createLiveFluid(fluidSource).push({ x: 8, y: 20, vx: 2 }).step().render(); // the same simulation, live const gif = animationGIF(project, 'idle', { scale: 8 }); // { data, width, height, notes, ... } const loop = folderGIF('shots/prism', { fps: 25 }); // GIF from numbered PNG frames; framesGIF takes RGBA frames const grid = frameGrid(project, 30); // durations off a 30 fps video frame grid ``` `src/core.js`, `src/craft.js`, `src/font.js`, `src/patch.js`, `src/fx.js`, `src/fluid.js` and `src/gif.js` are browser-compatible and have no Node imports. The Node-only exporter uses the standard library for compression and file output. The studio shares the same renderer as the CLI and MCP server. ## Develop and verify ```sh npm test npm run demo ``` Tests cover pixels, alpha blending, inheritance, transformations, flood fill, text and the font, dither (including value noise), palette ramps and shading, outlines, rewrite rules, cleanup, rotation, tweens, particle effects, fluid simulation (golden recipes per preset, palette-only output, loop seams), tilemaps and rule tiles, scene cues, attachments and sorting, schema alignment, packing, timing, PNG/APNG structure, GIF structure and decoding, video frame timing and placement, inspection sheets and grids, patching and comparison, revisions, overwrite protection, CLI stdin/errors, MCP calls, the Canvas runtime, the local server and the portable Windows build. `node scripts/qa-studio.mjs` walks the studio in a real browser (an installed Edge or Chrome, headless, with a throwaway profile; Node.js 22+): every sample, live editing, a broken recipe, the preview controls, Save, Open, Export and GIF downloads landing on disk, a recipe that links a shared palette file, draft recovery, keyboard access, narrow and wide windows, and that no request leaves the computer. `node scripts/verify-godot.mjs` loads exported SpriteFrames in a headless Godot 4, when one is installed, and checks every frame's region, trim margin, pixels and timing and each animation's playback. Optional independent checks use Pillow and Python's ZIP reader: `python scripts/verify-exports.py` after `npm run demo`; it also decodes GIFs (including ones made from PNG folders) and an image sequence and compares every pixel, delay and loop flag, and runs the sequence's ffmpeg command when ffmpeg is installed. The studio binds to `127.0.0.1`, serves an explicit asset allowlist, rejects foreign Host/Origin headers, and never writes through its HTTP API. Unsaved edits are kept as a draft in the browser's own storage for the studio's address, one per tab, and offered back after a reload or, once that tab is closed, on the next visit; nothing about them is sent to the server, and **Save JSON** remains the way to keep a recipe. Browser storage is per address, so a draft made on one port is not seen on another. Projects are limited to animation frames of 1024 pixels a side and 262,144 pixels (stills up to 4096 a side), 256 frames, 4,194,304 source pixels, 16,777,216 atlas pixels and bounded drawing/export work. This is designed for small sprites, effects and tiles. ## Pixelbolt Studio: portable builds `scripts/build-studio.mjs` packs the toolkit, the official Node.js 24 LTS runtime and a few small launcher scripts into one archive per system, for people who have no Node.js, git or administrator rights: a ZIP for 64-bit Windows, and a `.tar.gz` that keeps execute permissions for Linux (x64 and ARM64) and macOS (Apple silicon and Intel). Nothing is installed, and deleting the folder removes everything. **Download:** each release's page carries the five archives and a `PixelboltStudio--SHA256SUMS.txt` list, from 0.17.0 on: [the latest release](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/releases/latest). `.github/workflows/studio-assets.yml` builds, checks and attaches them once the Release workflow has finished. To check a download, run `sha256sum -c --ignore-missing PixelboltStudio--SHA256SUMS.txt` in its folder, or compare `Get-FileHash` on Windows. | | Studio | Command line | Connect an agent | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Windows | double-click `Pixelbolt Studio.cmd`, or drag a recipe onto it | `pixelbolt.cmd` | `Connect your agent.cmd` | | macOS | double-click `Pixelbolt Studio.command`, or `./pixelbolt-studio [recipe]` | `./pixelbolt` | `Connect your agent.command` or `./connect-your-agent` | | Linux | `./pixelbolt-studio [recipe]` | `./pixelbolt` | `./connect-your-agent` | The studio launcher is `pixelbolt preview --open`: it opens the default browser on loopback port 4747, or on any free port when that one is taken (the usual port is what lets the studio's draft recovery find its draft again). The connect helper prints MCP settings for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex and Cursor with that folder's paths, plus a one-line `claude mcp add` and `codex mcp add` command written for that system's shells; the helper itself never edits a configuration file. ```sh node scripts/build-studio.mjs # this machine's own target, into dist/ node scripts/build-studio.mjs --target all # win-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, darwin-arm64, darwin-x64 node scripts/build-studio.mjs --target all --check # rebuild and compare with the archives in dist/ node scripts/verify-studio.mjs dist/PixelboltStudio--.zip # or .tar.gz ``` Any machine can build any target; each archive comes with its `.sha256` and a per-file manifest. An archive holds exactly the files `npm pack` ships (under `app/`), the runtime, and the files for its system from [packaging](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/blob/main/packaging): no demos, tests or development scripts. The runtimes are pinned in the build script by version and SHA-256, downloaded from nodejs.org on the first build (36 to 58 MB each, cached in `dist/.cache`; `--node-archive ` uses a copy you already have) and included unmodified; a mismatch stops the build. `BUILD-INFO.txt` inside names the Pixelbolt version, the source commit, the target and the runtime's hashes. A build refuses uncommitted changes to shipped files unless `--allow-dirty` marks it as a development build, and a release build takes every shipped file from the commit itself rather than the working copy. One commit gives the same file list and per-file hashes anywhere. Where a runtime is pinned for the building machine the packing runs under that runtime, and the archives then come out byte-identical whichever system builds them: every CI runner (Windows, Linux on x64 and ARM64, and macOS) builds all five and prints their hashes. `verify-studio.mjs` extracts an archive with the system's own tool into a folder whose path has a space and a non-ASCII character, and runs it with no Node.js or git on `PATH`: the launcher (several copies, loopback only, every studio route, foreign Host and Origin refused, export, a recipe handed to it), the commands exactly as `START HERE.txt` gives them in two shells, the MCP server over stdio, the helper's output and its one-line commands, execute permissions and line endings, and that no process is left behind. It needs the system the archive is for; elsewhere it checks the contents only and says so. The Tests workflow builds, rebuilds and verifies each archive on a runner of its own system (the Intel Mac build on an Intel Mac runner), then runs the test suite on the bundled runtime and walks the extracted build's studio in the runner's browser. On the macOS runner the command line also runs with the download quarantine mark set. No runner has a person at the screen: the prompts Windows and macOS show for downloaded files, a double-click and a real browser are not exercised there. ## Contributing Bug reports, recipe examples, documentation improvements and focused pull requests are welcome. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/blob/main/AGENTS.md) before changing the toolkit. Report reproducible bugs through [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/skulitom/Pixelbolt/issues). ## Sibling tools Pixelbolt is one of five free, MIT-licensed tools for agents by the same author. Each runs locally and works as an MCP server: - [Anode](https://github.com/skulitom/Anode): Windows desktop automation in a hidden background session, so an agent can click, type and take screenshots without taking over your screen. - [Cutbolt](https://github.com/skulitom/Cutbolt): a video editing engine with exact timelines, captions and rendering. - [Inkbolt](https://github.com/skulitom/Inkbolt): vector and raster image editing for diagrams and illustrations, with SVG import and SVG or PDF export. - [Nestbolt](https://github.com/skulitom/Nestbolt): 2D nesting of parts on sheets for laser, CNC, plasma and waterjet cutting, also [in your browser](https://skulitom.github.io/Nestbolt/). ## License [MIT licensed](LICENSE). Included artwork is original and covered by the same license.

Pixel art and sprite animation that your AI agent can make, check and fix. Effect guides: fire, explosions, smoke and steam, water, slime and honey, and magic, each with recipes that open in the playground. Using Unreal Engine? Six free pixel art waterfall sprite sheets: one simulated waterfall in stone, lava, slime and moonlit, with Godot 4 files.

Try it. You need Node.js 20 or newer; there is nothing else to install, no API key and no network service:

cd Pixelbolt

Give it to your agent. For Claude Code, one line installs the pixel art skill, with nothing to clone and no MCP server (Pixelbolt 0.9.2 or later):

How it works

Write a JSON recipe with palettes, text grids, reusable symbols and drawing operations. Get transparent PNGs, sprite sheets, animated PNGs, GIFs for sharing, numbered frames for video editors, and the metadata and player needed to use them. Inspect and edit the recipe in a local browser studio.

Zero runtime dependencies. No build step, API key, image model, network service or native graphics library. Requires Node.js 20 or newer. Works from a checkout on Windows, macOS and Linux.

Fluid effects

Open http://127.0.0.1:4747, or add --open to have your default browser opened for you. If that port is in use, a free one is taken and printed instead; --port N insists on one port and fails when it is busy. preview hero.pixel.json starts with your own recipe. Pick the forest spirit, campfire or coin; edit the JSON; inspect the animation or sprite sheet; download the asset ZIP. The studio includes playback speed, frame selection, whole-number zoom (the scroll wheel zooms at the pointer, dragging pans, and + − 0 and F zoom, fit and go full screen), a pixel grid, onion skinning, palette inspection, source save/open, a GIF download of the current animation, numbered frames for a video editor, recovery of unsaved edits and live error messages. All assets and fonts are local.

![Pixelbolt's local studio showing the forest spirit sprite, animation frames, editable JSON recipe and palette](docs/images/studio.png)

Or generate an asset without opening a browser:


node bin/pixelbolt.js init hero.pixel.json

node bin/pixelbolt.js validate hero.pixel.json

node bin/pixelbolt.js inspect hero.pixel.json --out hero-frames.png

node bin/pixelbolt.js render hero.pixel.json --out output/hero

inspect saves a contact sheet of every frame and lists each frame's timing (--animation walk --every 100 draws a cell per 100 ms of playback, so pacing shows). Add --grid to read frames back as palette-key text; --animation, --frames (names or patterns such as 'flash-*') and --region narrow the view, and --step 2 --offset 1 keeps every second cell from the second, so a strobe's A and B frames can be read apart. validate hero.pixel.json --fps 30 also lists the durations that are not whole video frames at that rate and what a video sequence would do to each animation. patch hero.pixel.json --changes fix.json previews targeted edits and reports every pixel they change; add --out to save the new recipe. gif hero.pixel.json --out hero.gif saves one animation as a GIF for sharing. Command results except help and the preview server are JSON. Errors go to stderr and exit with code 1. Use - instead of a filename to read JSON from stdin. Existing output files are protected; add --force to replace them. A forced export over an earlier export of the same recipe or sequence also removes the frames it no longer has and lists them as removed; a sprite export removes only frame and animation PNGs its own earlier atlas lists and no other atlas in the folder does, so another sprite's frames and PNGs you add there aren't deleted. No command writes over a file it reads, even with --force and through a link or another spelling of its path; patch may save over the recipe it edits. No export writes over its own recipe or the files it references. You can optionally run npm link for the pixelbolt command. No npm install is needed.

pixelbolt share <recipe.json|-> prints a playground link to the source, including wave, crystal, falling-sand and rigid-body sources, which the playground compiles and keeps editable; render and scene accept --embed-recipe (recipes up to 1 MiB, so every PNG still opens in Pillow), recovered with import image.png --embedded --out recipe.json.

Both carry the resolved recipe text and engine version: the link in its URL fragment, which browsers do not send to a server, and the PNG in a compressed recipe chunk.

Export bundle

| File | Use |

| --- | --- |

| name.png | RGBA PNG sprite sheet, with configurable columns, padding and integer scale, or packed by visible bounds with sheet.trim |

| name.atlas.json | TexturePacker-style JSON hash: rectangles, trim offsets, source sizes, pivots/anchors, named points, frame durations, named animations and Aseprite-style frame tags. Stills and a still tile set (below) list their frames only, with no animations and no meta.frameTags |

| name.tres | Godot 4 SpriteFrames for AnimatedSprite2D: one atlas texture per frame (trimmed frames keep their place on the canvas) and every animation with its loop and exact frame times; keep it next to name.png. Not for stills or a still tile set |

| name.tileset.tres | Only for a tile set (an autotile set, or frames with tile): a Godot 4 TileSet for TileMapLayer with a terrain per set (blob, cardinal or corner, or a corner set of layered terrains whose transitions Godot paints), so Godot's terrain painter picks the tile Pixelbolt's tilemap would, plus each tile's probability and collision; keep it next to name.png. A tile set without animations of its own skips the SpriteFrames, APNGs, CSS and player |

| name.tsx | Only for a tile set: a Tiled tileset over name.png with a Wang set per terrain for the Terrain Brush (mixed for blob, edge for cardinal, corner for corner and layered sets), each tile's probability, collision objects and animation; keep it next to name.png |

| frames/*.png | Each frame as a transparent PNG |

| animations/*.png | APNG for each animation, retaining transparency, frame timing and loop behavior. Not for stills or a still tile set |

| name.css | CSS animation classes; supports multi-row sheets and unequal frame durations. Not for stills or a still tile set |

| player.js | Small, dependency-free Canvas player with play, pause, resume and named animations, plus loadSpriteSheet, frameAt and drawFrame for games. Not for stills or a still tile set |

| name.pixel.json | Editable source recipe |

| preview.html | Standalone preview you can open directly in a browser (the sheet, for stills and a still tile set) |

Stills are a recipe whose "animations" is {}: icons, UI states, a 9-slice panel. A still tile set is a tile set whose recipe leaves animations out. Neither plays anything, so the export writes only name.png, name.atlas.json (frames only), frames/, name.pixel.json, preview.html and README.txt (plus name.tileset.tres and name.tsx for a tile set), and no GIFs.

APNG files use the .png extension intentionally. Recipes can share a palette file ("palette": { "$ref": "palette.json" }), recolor keys per frame for palette cycling or per layer for a flash that leaves the rest of the frame alone, copy rectangles from template symbols or earlier frames (with exact colour swaps), outline layers (outside, inside or both, with direction masks for rim lights and drop shadows), dither between colours with canvas-anchored Bayer, custom, seeded non-periodic noise or clumping value-noise patterns, shade along palette ramps (ramps and the shade operation) without leaving the palette, draw whole character maps with the tilemap operation (variants, weights and neighbour rules), and grow detail such as moss or cracks with seeded rewrite rules. They compile 47-tile blob or 16-tile cardinal autotile sets with pixelbolt autotile, drawn from template rows or from a terrain description (a seamless fill and each side's edge, outline, rim light, shadow and tufts), optionally with shape variants, and review every tile over a test map with seam warnings; see the [authoring guide](docs/agent-guide.md) and [art workflow](docs/art-workflow.md#autotile-templates).

Several of these ideas come from Pixel Composer's node set, adapted to text recipes. Patches can propose De-Corner/De-Stray cleanup, and inspection diagnostics count per frame what it would change. Pose sources rotate parts by any angle into editable symbols, using RotSprite-style resampling that adds no colours, and tween eased in-betweens. Scene trajectories ease. A pixelforge-fx source compiles seeded particle emitters and spell shapes (slashes, shockwave rings, beams, lightning, magic circles, impact stars, fireballs, cel-shaded water streams and drops) into an ordinary recipe with pixelbolt compile, a pixelforge-fluid source does the same with a fluid simulation, and a pixelforge-normals source derives a lighting normal pass from any recipe: an editable recipe aligned frame for frame, for scene lighting and engine normal maps ([the spirit's](examples/forest-spirit.normals.json), lit in [a small night scene](examples/forest-spirit-lit.scene.json); [details](docs/art-workflow.md#generated-normal-passes)). See [the shrine](examples/shrine.json), [the swing](examples/swing.poses.json), [the effects](examples/effects.fx.json) and [a healing circle](examples/healing-circle.fx.json). Lossless PNG import is supported (RGB, RGBA, greyscale and indexed, up to 8 bits per channel, not interlaced), optionally with unscaled atlas timing metadata; see [interchange limits](docs/art-workflow.md#lossless-raster-return-path). GIF import, native Aseprite files and automatic quantization remain outside the current scope. Sources stay editable JSON.

GIF for sharing

APNG keeps full alpha and exact timing, but many chat, forum and store pages only animate GIFs and cannot scale pixels crisply. pixelbolt gif writes one animation as a GIF at the frames' own size; --scale (1-16) enlarges it by a whole number for pages that would show a small sprite tiny:


node bin/pixelbolt.js gif hero.pixel.json --out hero.gif

node bin/pixelbolt.js gif --preset campfire --size 32x32 --scale 8 --out campfire.gif --sheet campfire-frames.png

node bin/pixelbolt.js gif hero.pixel.json --animation blink --scale 8 --background "#17191d" --out hero-blink.gif

Colours are exact: nothing is quantized or dithered, and a frame that needs more than 256 colours is refused with an error instead of being approximated. GIF has no partial transparency, so pixels below 50% alpha become transparent and the rest opaque; --background (a palette name or opaque hex colour) blends every pixel onto one colour instead, which keeps soft shadows. Frame times are rounded to GIF's 10 ms steps with the remainder carried to the next frame, and raised to 20 ms where shorter. Transparent pixels stay clear in every viewer, including ffmpeg and Pillow, which fill a cleared frame with the background colour unless it names a transparent index (the notes report the rare frame with 256 colours of its own that has none to name). The JSON result's notes say which of these happened. The studio's GIF button downloads the current animation at the current zoom, and MCP pixel_render takes "gif": {} (the frames' own size) or "gif": { "scale": 8 }. Every render also reports a check of what it wrote; give pixel_render an expect (or render an --expect) with the size, frames, colours, background or loop the user asked for, and the check names each file that misses it and how to fix it. The export bundle itself is unchanged.

pixelbolt gif-frames makes a GIF from a folder of numbered PNG frames, such as a sequence folder or frames a video or effects tool wrote, by the same rules:


node bin/pixelbolt.js gif-frames shots/prism --fps 25 --out prism.gif

node bin/pixelbolt.js gif-frames shots/prism --fps 30 --loops 3 --background "#101828" --prefix prism_ --out prism-3x.gif

Files are read in number order (prism_0001.png, prism_0002.png …); gaps in the numbering, other PNGs in the folder and a folder holding two sequences (choose one with --prefix) are reported, never guessed around. Each frame keeps its exact colours: one with more than 256 is refused by name, and when the frames use different colours, each frame carries a colour table of its own, so a loop of 48 frames at 1080 × 1080 with about 120 colours per frame and 4,345 in all decodes back pixel for pixel, where a palette generator would shift some colours. Frame k starts at k × 1000 / fps ms rounded to GIF's centiseconds: 25 fps is 40 ms per frame, 30 fps alternates 30 and 40 ms and keeps the loop's length, and above 50 fps delays are raised to 20 ms, which the notes report with the new length. --loops is the number of plays, 0 (the default) for ever. Without transparency, each frame after the first stores only the rectangle that changed. The PNGs may be RGB, RGBA, greyscale or indexed with up to 8 bits per channel, all the same size; the loop may hold 134,217,728 pixels (115 frames at 1080 × 1080).

Pixel text

The text operation draws titles, captions, labels and counters in a built-in pixel font: printable ASCII, the accented letters of western European languages (À–ÿ, Œ œ Š š Ž ž Ÿ), Cyrillic, Japanese kana, every Korean Hangul syllable, 165 ideographs of game menus (開始, 設定, 魔法 …) and common symbols such as € £ © — … “ ” „ « », with capitals 7 pixels tall, proportional letters and tabular digits. Hangul and ideographs are drawn in a 9×9 cell. The accent of a capital sits in the two rows above y.


{ "op": "text", "x": 120, "y": 8, "text": "GAME OVER\nscore 12480", "color": "ink", "align": "center" }

align says whether x is the left edge, the centre or the right edge; spacing, lineHeight, scale and rotation adjust it, and outline after it gives a readable edge. Text that runs off the canvas is reported like any other clipped drawing, and a character the font lacks is an error that names it. [examples/caption.json](examples/caption.json) is a lower third that opens and types its title; node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence examples/caption.json --fps 30 --size 1080p --align bottom --offset 0,-64 --out shots/caption turns it into 81 frames that sit across the bottom of a 1080p picture.

Frames for a video editor

Video editors do not animate APNG, and GIF loses alpha and exact timing. pixelbolt sequence writes what editors do read: one numbered PNG per video frame, at a constant frame rate, on a canvas of the video's size, with the alpha kept.


node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence hero.pixel.json --fps 30 --size 1080p --out shots/hero

node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence examples/effects.fx.json --animation sparks --fps 29.97 --size 4k --scale 16 --align bottom --offset 0,-200 --out shots/sparks

node bin/pixelbolt.js sequence room.scene.json --fps 24 --size 1080p --fit cover --out shots/room
  • Timing. Each video frame shows the pose that is active when the frame starts. --fps takes 24, 25, 30, 50, 60, the NTSC rates 23.976, 29.97 and 59.94 (kept exact as 24000/1001, 30000/1001 and 60000/1001, so long clips do not drift), or a fraction. --loops n or --seconds s sets the length; --step 2 animates on twos. A looping animation keeps cycling; one that plays once holds its last pose.
  • Size. --size is 720p, 1080p, 1440p, 4k, vertical (1080×1920), square or WIDTHxHEIGHT. The sprite is enlarged by a whole number, never resampled: the largest that fits, or --scale up to 256. --align (top-left … center … bottom-right) and --offset x,y place it. --fit cover takes the smallest whole number that covers the canvas instead and crops what hangs over; --align then chooses the part that stays, and the result's placement.visible says which columns and rows of the source that is. Without --size the canvas is the sprite at --scale. --background blends onto an opaque colour instead of keeping alpha.
  • Sources. A recipe (--animation picks one), a pose, autotile or effects source, which is compiled on the way in, or a scene, which is rendered moment by moment as a shot; moments that look the same share one PNG. A scene of 192×108 or 240×135 pixels fills 1080p exactly at scale 10 or 8. Any other scene is centred with margins in its own background colour, so the shot is still opaque from edge to edge, or fills the canvas with --fit cover.
  • What you get. A new folder with name_0001.png onwards, sequence.json (frame rate as a fraction, frame count, size, placement, loop facts and the timing of every pose) and a README.txt that says how to import them. The result's notes say what the frame grid did: which poses changed length, which are shorter than a video frame and never shown, and whether the clip ends exactly where the loop does, with the number of loops that would.
  • One video file. Pixelbolt does not encode video. The folder's README and the JSON result give the exact ffmpeg command for a ProRes 4444 .mov with alpha, and, when there is a background, for an H.264 .mp4 in lossless 4:4:4. H.264 usually stores colour once for each 2 × 2 pixels (4:2:0), which smears every pixel edge whatever the scale once a player interpolates it; 4:4:4 keeps every colour, in a file no larger for pixel art, but QuickTime, Safari and Windows' own players may not play it, so on an even canvas h264Compatible gives a 4:2:0 file as well. With ffmpeg 7 the ProRes command keeps the alpha exactly and the colours within 2 of 255, and the H.264 command the colours within 1; scripts/verify-exports.py repeats those checks when ffmpeg is installed.

In the editor, import the files as an image sequence and set the clip's frame rate (the files carry none), then leave the clip at 100% scale: scaling there would blur the pixels. A sequence holds at most 18,000 frames and a canvas at most 4096 pixels on a side. MCP pixel_render and pixel_scene take "sequence": { "fps": 30, "size": "1080p" } with the same options.

The studio's Frames button downloads the same files for the animation on screen as one ZIP. Its dialog also shows the pixelbolt sequence command and the MCP sequence argument for the chosen frame rate and size, so an agent can repeat the export without the browser.

Large frames and stills

An animation frame may be up to 1024 pixels a side and 262,144 pixels: a full-screen 320 × 180, 480 × 270 or 640 × 360 overlay (rain, snow, fog) is one recipe, as is a 512 × 512 or 1024 × 256 frame. All of a recipe's frames hold at most 4,194,304 pixels, so 72 frames of 320 × 180, 18 of 640 × 360 or 16 of 512 × 512. A recipe with a single frame may be larger still: up to 4096 pixels a side and 4,194,304 pixels in all. A 1920 × 1080 or 2560 × 1440 backdrop, wallpaper or mural is then one canvas, drawn at one screen pixel per art pixel, and every drawing operation sees all of it. On a canvas wider or taller than 256, rectangles, ellipses and dither or shade regions may be up to twice its side instead of 512.

A scene's view and each of its assets, an effect source and an imported frame have the animation frame's limit, so a tiled level is one picture. Everything else keeps its limits: pose, bodies, crystal, normals and compiled powder sources stay at 256 pixels a side, fluid and wave sources at 128, and the 67-million-pixel drawing budget is unchanged: fill, replace and outline each pass over the whole canvas, about 2 million of that budget at 1920 × 1080. To show bigger pixels instead, enlarge a small canvas with sheet.scale or sequence --size, as before. The studio opens a large still or an animation frame over 256 px a side fitted to its window (zoom 1 shows it at 1×), scaled down smoothly so dither reads as the tone it makes; zoom in with the scroll wheel and drag to look around at 1× and up.

Saves its recipe revision.
  • pixel_patch: apply targeted set, insert, remove and paint edits. For example, { "paint": "frames[blink]", "value": [{ "x": 9, "y": 7, "color": "k" }] } corrects a pixel in final canvas coordinates after all layers; transparent erases it. Returns every frame whose pixels changed (exact pixels for small edits) and a before/after PNG. The source stays unchanged and successful edits get a new revision.
  • pixel_render: render { "project": ... }, return a PNG contact sheet of every frame with cell names/timing plus the output folder, its key files and frame/animation counts (listFiles: true lists everything). Add "animation": "idle" to preview a sequence in playback order. The exported APNGs and HTML preview play the animation. Every call writes a fresh folder inside the configured output directory.
  • pixel_compile: compile a pixelforge-poses source (including bones, masses, relative joints, reach targets and editable motion templates), a pixelforge-autotile template or terrain (returned with a second image of every tile over a test map), a pixelforge-fx source (particles and spell shapes), a pixelforge-fluid source (simulated smoke, fire, explosions, magic, water, thick and sticky liquids, sand, air pockets and bubbles, ice and steam, electric arcs, and bodies that float, sink and stir), a pixelforge-wave source (looping interference and portals), a pixelforge-crystal source (crystals, clusters, geodes and snowflakes that grow and rest), a pixelforge-powder source (a falling-sand sandbox of sand, water, fire, smoke, lava and more, sampled into one-shot clips), a pixelforge-bodies source (balls, boxes and hoops that bounce, stack and rest, and territory matches; sequence writes a match of any length as numbered video frames) or a pixelforge-normals source (a normal pass derived from a recipe or revision, with flat faces by colour for boxes and walls) into a recipe revision, with a contact sheet and optional metadata; preset compiles a shipped preset by name instead of a source.
  • pixel_scene: render a pixelforge-scene manifest (tilemaps with autotile legends and neighbour rules, named cues, sequences, trajectories, attachments, ground sorting, shade placements, ramp or multiplied lighting from point lights and a sun, with cast shadows, palette themes, haze for far planes, a panning camera with parallax planes) at any time, with a depth view of what is drawn in front of what, export it (with a Tiled map of it whose layers carry each plane's parallax, scene.tmx, hazed copies of far assets, and each plane as an image that a Godot scene.tscn scrolls with Parallax2D), or write it as a shot of numbered PNG frames with sequence; assets may be revisions.

pixel_render optionally accepts "share": true for a playground link (or a link-limit error without failing the render) and "embedRecipe": true for recipes inside exported PNGs.

pixel_render also writes files at the names the user asked for: "saveAs": { "sheet": "assets/hero.png", "gif": "assets/hero.gif" } (keys sheet, atlas, godot for the Godot .tres, tileset for an autotile set's Godot TileSet, tiled for its Tiled tileset, recipe, gif, apng or any exported PNG, GIF or JSON file; paths inside the server root, keeping the file type, never under a hidden name or in the home folder's AppData or Library). A saved atlas, .tres or .tsx names the saved sheet (or the export folder's), and a .tres inside a Godot project needs its sheet inside it too. It never replaces an existing file unless "overwrite": true, and then a JSON file only if it is a recipe, atlas or sequence, a .tres only if it is the same kind of Godot resource (SpriteFrames, TileSet or CanvasTexture), and a .tsx only if it is a Tiled tileset; it never writes over the palette and asset files the recipe references, and checks every path before writing anything.

pixel_patch also supports compact grid, masked move, regional recolor and proposed cleanup of doubled corners and stray pixels, with explicit frame or inherited scope, and applies saved correction overlays (overlay). Large pixel_render previews are sampled with total/shown/omitted metadata instead of blocking a valid export; exported animations remain complete. Palette and scene file references resolve inside the server's --root (default: its working directory); requests may be up to 16 MiB, and an oversized request is answered with an error without stopping the server. Each tool call runs in a worker thread and is stopped if it takes longer than 50 seconds (--time-limit <seconds> changes this) or runs out of memory; the call is answered with an error that says so, and the server keeps serving. A sequence from one call may come to at most 512 MB; pixelbolt sequence writes longer shots.

Send a recipe once. Each successful recipe-tool response includes a revision id that the other tools accept in place of project, so later calls, including patches, need not resend the recipe. Validate, inspect, patch and render save immutable snapshots in <MCP --out directory>/.revisions/; they survive restarts when you use the same directory, even before an asset export. Once that directory exists, the presets listing keeps what it measured in .presets/ beside them, so later listings are quick. Prefer an absolute --out path. Earlier revisions remain undo points. Older rendered revisions can be recovered from saved bundle recipes. Render also saves the recipe beside the assets.

The server implements newline-delimited stdio MCP with initialization, version negotiation, ping and tool discovery/calls. It supports protocol versions 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18 and 2025-11-25 through initialization, plus 2026-07-28 through server/discover and stateless requests carrying protocol version and client capabilities in _meta. It uses no HTTP transport or external services. See the MCP stdio specification.

An agent can also use the CLI directly. The reusable [agent skill](skills/pixelbolt-pixel-art/SKILL.md) and [authoring reference](docs/agent-guide.md) explain the complete format; npx -y pixelbolt@latest skill install gives Claude Code the skill with its guides, schemas and examples and no server. [schema.json](schema.json) supports editor completion and structural validation; the rasterizer additionally validates references, matching row widths and resource limits.

Or use CSS alone:

CSS honors reduced-motion preferences. The Canvas API leaves autoplay decisions to the application. Atlas paths in SpritePlayer.load resolve relative to the atlas URL.

A game drawing many sprites into one canvas can use the same module's helpers. drawFrame places a frame by its anchor (when the recipe declares one), restores trimmed frames to their original offset and snaps fractional positions to whole pixels, so a sprite moving at sub-pixel speeds keeps hard edges. rotate (radians, about the anchor) turns it. A turned sprite keeps clean square pixels only where each of its pixels covers several of the canvas's, so draw what turns, and what should glide from place to place and not step, on a second canvas at the screen's own resolution with scale 3 or more, laid over the canvas the grid-aligned world is drawn on:


<script type="module">

  import { loadSpriteSheet, frameAt, drawFrame } from './assets/player.js';

  const hero = await loadSpriteSheet('./assets/hero.atlas.json'), context = canvas.getContext('2d');

  requestAnimationFrame(function draw(time) {

    context.clearRect(0, 0, canvas.width, canvas.height);

    drawFrame(context, hero, frameAt(hero.atlas, 'walk', time), 64, 96, { scale: 3 }); // (64, 96) is where the anchor lands

    requestAnimationFrame(draw);

  });

</script>

For Godot 4, put name.png and name.tres in one folder of the project and use the .tres as an AnimatedSprite2D's Sprite Frames, or install the [Godot addon](docs/game-integration.md#the-editor-addon-recipes-as-spriteframes), which imports *.pixel.json recipes as SpriteFrames and renders them again when they change. For another engine, use the atlas rectangles or individual PNGs. For regular-grid importers, set sheet.padding to 0 and use the exported frame dimensions. Phaser accepts the JSON-hash frame layout via load.atlas; named animation sequences are in the extra animations field. See [game integration notes](docs/game-integration.md).

JavaScript API


import { renderProject, inspectProject, patchRecipe, compareProjects, createBundle, writeBundle, readExpect, checkDelivery, compileEffects, compileFluid, createLiveFluid, animationGIF, folderGIF, frameGrid } from './src/index.js';



const project = renderProject(recipe); // RGBA buffers, durations, warnings

const view = inspectProject(project, { grid: true }); // contact sheet RGBA, palette-key grids

const { recipe: fire, metadata } = compileFluid(fluidSource); // a fluid simulation baked into palette grids

const { rgba, keys } = createLiveFluid(fluidSource).push({ x: 8, y: 20, vx: 2 }).step().render(); // the same simulation, live

const loop = folderGIF('shots/prism', { fps: 25 }); // GIF from numbered PNG frames; framesGIF takes RGBA frames

node scripts/build-studio.mjs                       # this machine's own target, into dist/

node scripts/build-studio.mjs --target all          # win-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, darwin-arm64, darwin-x64

node scripts/build-studio.mjs --target all --check  # rebuild and compare with the archives in dist/

node scripts/verify-studio.mjs dist/PixelboltStudio-<version>-<target>.zip   # or .tar.gz

Any machine can build any target; each archive comes with its .sha256 and a per-file manifest. An archive holds exactly the files npm pack ships (under app/), the runtime, and the files for its system from packaging: no demos, tests or development scripts. The runtimes are pinned in the build script by version and SHA-256, downloaded from nodejs.org on the first build (36 to 58 MB each, cached in dist/.cache; --node-archive <file> uses a copy you already have) and included unmodified; a mismatch stops the build. BUILD-INFO.txt inside names the Pixelbolt version, the source commit, the target and the runtime's hashes. A build refuses uncommitted changes to shipped files unless --allow-dirty marks it as a development build, and a release build takes every shipped file from the commit itself rather than the working copy. One commit gives the same file list and per-file hashes anywhere. Where a runtime is pinned for the building machine the packing runs under that runtime, and the archives then come out byte-identical whichever system builds them: every CI runner (Windows, Linux on x64 and ARM64, and macOS) builds all five and prints their hashes.

verify-studio.mjs extracts an archive with the system's own tool into a folder whose path has a space and a non-ASCII character, and runs it with no Node.js or git on PATH: the launcher (several copies, loopback only, every studio route, foreign Host and Origin refused, export, a recipe handed to it), the commands exactly as START HERE.txt gives them in two shells, the MCP server over stdio, the helper's output and its one-line commands, execute permissions and line endings, and that no process is left behind. It needs the system the archive is for; elsewhere it checks the contents only and says so. The Tests workflow builds, rebuilds and verifies each archive on a runner of its own system (the Intel Mac build on an Intel Mac runner), then runs the test suite on the bundled runtime and walks the extracted build's studio in the runner's browser. On the macOS runner the command line also runs with the download quarantine mark set. No runner has a person at the screen: the prompts Windows and macOS show for downloaded files, a double-click and a real browser are not exercised there.

Sibling tools

Pixelbolt is one of five free, MIT-licensed tools for agents by the same author. Each runs locally and works as an MCP server:

  • Anode: Windows desktop automation in a hidden background session, so an agent can click, type and take screenshots without taking over your screen.
  • Cutbolt: a video editing engine with exact timelines, captions and rendering.
  • Inkbolt: vector and raster image editing for diagrams and illustrations, with SVG import and SVG or PDF export.
  • Nestbolt: 2D nesting of parts on sheets for laser, CNC, plasma and waterjet cutting, also in your browser.
